passage: Before: On Monday at breakfast, Eshaan, two, sat on his grandfather's lap, tapping the newspaper. During: On Wednesday he tripped on the courtyard step and howled. His uncle Tanvir was nearest and scooped him up, and Eshaan sobbed into his shoulder, then quietened. A cousin pulled funny faces until he giggled. After: By Sunday evening he fell asleep on his grandmother's bed while the grown-ups talked, and nobody asked who had put him there.

qa.q: Whose lap did Eshaan sit on at breakfast?
qa.a: His grandfather's lap.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan calm down so quickly with his uncle?
qa.a: Tanvir is one of many familiar people he trusts, so comfort from whoever is nearest works.

qa.q: What is one strength of growing up with many caregivers?
qa.a: Comfort is always close by, and the child feels safe with several people.

qa.q: How might Eshaan's mother feel about his day?
qa.a: At ease, since many trusted relatives share his care.

grounding: It shows a toddler in a joint household soothed and cared for by many familiar people.

passage: In a big old house in Lucknow lived Ujjwal, two, with his parents, grandparents, two aunts and three cousins. When he slipped off the veranda step, his aunt Sharmila was nearest. She scooped him up and rocked him, humming. He cried a little, then rested his head on her chest. Soon his grandmother called, "Mango slices!" and he wriggled down and toddled off, sticky and smiling.

qa.q: Who was nearest when Ujjwal slipped off the step?
qa.a: His aunt Sharmila.

qa.q: How can you tell Ujjwal trusts Sharmila?
qa.a: He rested his head on her chest and calmed down quickly while she rocked him.

qa.q: What might a small family do to give a child several trusted adults?
qa.a: Invite grandparents, neighbours or friends to spend regular time with the child.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal's mother feel hearing about the fall later?
qa.a: Calm, since in a joint family another trusted adult was there to comfort him.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler in a joint family comforted by whoever is nearest.

passage: "Who's crying?" Dadi called from the kitchen. "It's Sangeeta," said her cousin Mahima, eight. "She dropped her doll in the bucket." "I'll get her," said Chachi. She lifted Sangeeta, two. "Mama?" Sangeeta sniffled. "Mama's at the market. Chachi is here." Sangeeta leaned on her shoulder and the sobs slowed. Then Dada called, "Sangeeta, come see the parrot on the wall!" She wriggled down and ran to him, doll forgotten.

qa.q: Where did Sangeeta drop her doll?
qa.a: In the bucket.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta's quick calm with Chachi show?
qa.a: That she feels safe with many family members, not only her mother.

qa.q: How does Mahima help, even though she is only eight?
qa.a: She tells the adults what happened, so the right help comes quickly.

qa.q: What would change if Sangeeta lived with only her parents?
qa.a: She might cry longer for her mother, since fewer familiar people would be nearby.

grounding: It shows a toddler in a joint family soothed by several caregivers.

passage: "I'm just getting water, Irfan," said Ammi, standing up. Irfan, two, wailed and grabbed her leg. "Ammi, no!" His father, Abbu, knelt beside him. "I'm here, beta." Irfan kept crying and reaching for the kitchen door. Rukmini aunty, visiting, laughed softly. "Ours was the same." Ammi came back with the glass. Irfan clung to her, hiccupping. The flat was quiet again.

qa.q: What did Ammi go to fetch?
qa.a: Water.

qa.q: Why was a one-minute absence so hard for Irfan?
qa.a: He is closely tied to his two parents, so even a short separation feels big to him.

qa.q: What could Ammi say before stepping away next time?
qa.a: Tell him exactly where she is going and that she will be right back, then return quickly.

qa.q: How does Rukmini aunty see Irfan's crying?
qa.a: As normal; she laughs softly because her own child was the same.

grounding: It shows a toddler in a nuclear home closely attached to his parents and upset when one leaves.

passage: Daycare note, week two. Jyoti, two, lives with just her mother and father. At drop-off she cries hard and holds her mother's dupatta for several minutes. Inside, she keeps glancing at the door. When her father, Vijay, arrives in the evening, she runs to him with a huge smile. Her bond with her parents looks deep. We will keep her mornings calm and give her one special teacher to stay close to.

qa.q: Who picks Jyoti up in the evening?
qa.a: Her father, Vijay.

qa.q: What do Jyoti's glances at the door suggest?
qa.a: She is waiting for her parents, because her strongest bonds are with them.

qa.q: Why might one special teacher help Jyoti?
qa.a: Building one new close bond is easier for her than trusting many new faces at once.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel when Jyoti runs to him?
qa.a: Loved and happy, maybe also relieved.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler in a nuclear family with deep, narrow bonds and sharp distress at separation.

passage: Tenzin, two, lived with only his parents above their shop in a hill town. When his mother stepped out to the post office, he stood at the window and cried loudly. His father, Deepak, left the counter, picked him up and showed him the street. "Amala is coming back soon." Tenzin kept pointing at the door. When his mother returned, he reached out and buried his face in her neck.

qa.q: Where did Tenzin's mother go?
qa.a: To the post office.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin keep crying even with his father there?
qa.a: He is tightly bonded to both parents, so his mother leaving still felt upsetting.

qa.q: What did Deepak do that helped a little?
qa.a: He held Tenzin, showed him the street and reassured him that his mother would come back.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's days differ in a big joint family?
qa.a: He would see many more faces and might cope more easily when one person leaves.

grounding: It shows a toddler in a nuclear home with close bonds and sharp distress when a parent leaves.

passage: At the community centre summer camp, Sumit, five, who lived with six cousins at home, handed his crayons to a new boy, Tarun, without being asked. When Tarun grabbed his biscuit, Sumit shouted, "Hey!" and pushed him. The camp leader stepped between them. "Hands are not for pushing." A minute later Sumit broke the biscuit in half and handed over a piece as if nothing had happened. Tarun, who had just joined, stared at the half-biscuit, puzzled that they were friends again so fast.

qa.q: How many cousins does Sumit live with?
qa.a: Six cousins.

qa.q: Why could Sumit share and make up so quickly?
qa.a: Living with many cousins, he is used to sharing freely and fighting and making up fast.

qa.q: How could the camp leader guide Sumit?
qa.a: Praise his generous sharing while helping him use words instead of pushing.

qa.q: Why might Tarun be puzzled?
qa.a: He is new and not used to a fight ending in shared food a minute later.

grounding: It shows a child from a big family sharing freely and fighting and making up quickly.

passage: I'm Kalyani's older cousin, and there are seven of us kids in Dada's house. Kalyani, five, shares a bed with two of us, and nobody ever asks her first. At tea time she hands out biscuits to everyone before taking one herself. Yesterday she fought with Chetan over the swing, and they both cried. Ten minutes later they were sharing a mango on the steps, juice everywhere. I don't think she knows what privacy means yet. She just knows we're all together.

qa.q: What were Kalyani and Chetan sharing on the steps?
qa.a: A mango.

qa.q: What does handing out biscuits first say about Kalyani?
qa.a: In a big household, sharing and belonging are simply taken for granted.

qa.q: What might Kalyani need as she grows older?
qa.a: A little space of her own, as privacy starts to matter.

qa.q: How does the older cousin see the quick fight and make-up?
qa.a: As a normal part of life in their big family.

grounding: It illustrates a child among cousins sharing everything and fighting and making up quickly.

passage: Before: In June, Amandeep, five, moved into his grandparents' house in Ludhiana with four cousins. At first he cried when they used his toys. During: By September he shared his bed with cousin Jagdish, passed rotis round the table without being told, fought over the TV remote, and made up within minutes. After: In December his school friend asked, "Do you have your own room?" Amandeep looked puzzled. "Why would I?"

qa.q: How many cousins did Amandeep live with?
qa.a: Four cousins.

qa.q: Why was Amandeep puzzled by his friend's question?
qa.a: In a shared home, belonging is taken for granted and privacy is not yet something he needs. 😊

qa.q: What helped Amandeep adjust after crying in June?
qa.a: Living closely with cousins every day taught him to share and make up quickly.

qa.q: How might the friend who has their own room see Amandeep's answer?
qa.a: As surprising, since their home life is very different.

grounding: It shows a child learning to share space and make up quickly in a joint household.

passage: Before: When her son's family moved in, Chandrika Paati, seventy, prayed alone every dawn, lamp in hand. During: Within weeks her grandson Dhruv, nine, sat beside her, copying the words and the way she folded her hands. At night he begged for stories about her village. He started using her old sayings at school: "Slow water cuts stone." After: One morning Paati noticed him teaching the prayer to a neighbour's child. Something warm rose in her chest. Her son said, "In our Delhi flat, he'd never have learned this." Paati smiled. "Children learn what they see every day."

qa.q: What saying did Dhruv start using at school?
qa.a: Slow water cuts stone.

qa.q: What did Paati feel when she saw Dhruv teaching the prayer?
qa.a: A warm pride, as if her role in the family had real meaning again. 😊

qa.q: How could a nuclear family pass on such traditions?
qa.a: Deliberately set aside time with grandparents, through visits, calls or shared rituals.

qa.q: What might these dawn prayers mean to Dhruv?
qa.a: A special daily closeness with his grandmother, and a way into her world.

grounding: It shows a grandmother noticing her grandchild copying her prayers and sayings, giving her role meaning.

passage: Sit, Himani, let me tell you something. When you and Chinmay were small and we all lived together, I never thought much about teaching you. Then one afternoon I heard you singing my old harvest song to your dolls, word for word. The same week, Chinmay told his teacher my saying about patience and the mango tree. My heart filled up. Your parents were busy at the bank all day. I had time, and you had me. Now you are grown. When you have children, find ways for them to sit near their elders every day, not only on festivals.

qa.q: What song did Himani sing to her dolls?
qa.a: The grandparent's old harvest song.

qa.q: What made the grandparent's heart fill up?
qa.a: Realising the children had absorbed their songs and sayings just by living together.

qa.q: What advice does the grandparent give Himani?
qa.a: When she has children, let them sit near their elders every day, not only on festivals. ❤️

qa.q: How might Himani feel hearing this story now?
qa.a: Touched, and more aware of what her grandparent gave her.

grounding: It illustrates a grandparent noticing grandchildren absorbing songs and sayings through daily contact.

passage: With the power cut on a hot evening, there was no TV and no fan. Grandma Mahima, in her small house in Goa, lit an oil lamp and began telling stories to her grandsons, Anand, ten, and Sunny, eight. Sunny repeated her Konkani phrases, giggling at the funny ones. Anand asked about the old fishing boats. Mahima watched them and felt useful in a way she hadn't since her husband died. Their parents, who lived in the city, rarely had time for these stories. She decided to tell one every visit, power cut or not.

qa.q: What did Grandma Mahima light?
qa.a: An oil lamp.

qa.q: Why did Mahima feel useful that evening?
qa.a: She saw her grandsons eagerly learning her language and stories, giving her role meaning after her husband's death.

qa.q: What small habit did Mahima decide on?
qa.a: Telling one story every visit, power cut or not.

qa.q: What is the evening like for Sunny?
qa.a: Fun and close; he giggles while repeating her Konkani phrases.

grounding: It shows a grandmother noticing her grandchildren learning her language and stories, which gives her role meaning.

passage: In a flat in Dubai, where his family had moved from Hyderabad, five-year-old Jamal met his father's colleague for the first time. "Say hello to Kaito uncle," said his mother. "Hello Kaito," said Jamal. His mother whispered, "Kaito uncle." Jamal repeated it, frowning. Kaito laughed warmly and ruffled his hair. The next day Jamal called the older girl next door "Maryam didi" without being told. She beamed and gave him a date from her bag. Jamal didn't know why, but the extra word made people happy.

qa.q: What did Maryam give Jamal?
qa.a: A date from her bag.

qa.q: Why did Jamal start adding titles on his own?
qa.a: He noticed they made people smile, even before he understood what they meant. 😊

qa.q: How could his parents explain the titles?
qa.a: Tell him simply that uncle and didi are warm, respectful ways to address older people.

qa.q: Why did Kaito laugh when Jamal said his name alone?
qa.a: He found it sweet and was not offended, knowing Jamal is small and learning.

grounding: It shows a child copying honorifics like uncle and didi before understanding their warmth and rank.

passage: In the KG classroom, Mr. Akash taught the children to say "Good morning, Ma'am" and to call the helpers "Didi" and "Bhaiya". Five-year-old Kiran kept calling the helper by her name, "Shanti!" Mr. Akash said gently, "Shanti didi." Kiran repeated it, puzzled. Later, when Shanti didi knelt to tie her shoelace, Kiran said, "Thank you, Shanti didi," and hugged her knees. Shanti didi's face lit up.

qa.q: What did the children learn to call the helpers?
qa.a: Didi and Bhaiya.

qa.q: Why was Kiran puzzled when corrected?
qa.a: She was just copying sounds and did not yet understand why the title mattered.

qa.q: Which part of Mr. Akash's approach worked?
qa.a: Correcting gently by modelling the words, so Kiran learned by repeating rather than feeling scolded.

qa.q: What might being called Shanti didi mean to the helper?
qa.a: It shows warmth and respect, which is why her face lit up.

grounding: It illustrates a child learning honorifics by copying before understanding the warmth they carry.

passage: I'm Jasleen's aunt, and at the family wedding I watched her learn something. Jasleen, four, had been told to say "Sat Sri Akal ji" to all the elders. She said it fast, like a game, "Satsriakalji!", to everyone, even a waiter. The elders laughed and patted her head. When her cousin Rafiq arrived, she shouted, "Veerji!" and jumped on him. I don't think she knows what the words mean yet. But she knows they make people smile, and she says them with so much warmth.

qa.q: Who did Jasleen jump on?
qa.a: Her cousin Rafiq.

qa.q: What does Jasleen seem to understand about the greetings?
qa.a: That they make people smile, although she does not yet know what they mean.

qa.q: How could the family help her learn the meaning?
qa.a: Explain simply that these words show love and respect for elders and older cousins. 🙂

qa.q: How might the waiter feel being greeted that way?
qa.a: Probably amused and touched by the cheerful greeting.

grounding: It shows a child copying respectful greetings with warmth before understanding their meaning.

passage: School counsellor's note, Class 5. Francis, ten, came in upset after a family lunch. He had checked the prices of rice at two shops and told his uncle which one was cheaper. His uncle said, "Respect your elders," and the table went quiet. Francis asked me, "But I was right. Why does respect mean I have to shut up?" I told him being polite and caring is what matters; being afraid is not the point. We practised a line: "Uncle, I checked. Can I show you?" His classmate Ishita, waiting outside, said she'd had the same problem at home. I'll run a class session on polite disagreement next week.

qa.q: What had Francis checked before lunch?
qa.a: The prices of rice at two shops.

qa.q: Why was Francis upset by respect your elders?
qa.a: It seemed to mean he must stay silent even when right, and no reason was given.

qa.q: What line did the counsellor help him practise?
qa.a: Uncle, I checked. Can I show you?, which keeps both his manners and his voice.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel hearing a class session is planned?
qa.a: Relieved that her problem is shared and will be discussed. 🙂

grounding: It shows a child told to respect elders without reasons and learning respect means courtesy, not fear.

passage: Dear Diary, Today Dadi said girls shouldn't whistle. I asked why. Mummy said, "Respect your elders, Damini." That's what everyone says when they don't have a reason! I felt angry and small, like my question was bad. Later Papa explained that respect means being kind and polite to Dadi, not being scared to ask. He said I can ask, "Dadi, why?" in a soft voice. So I did, at dinner. Dadi laughed and said her own mother told her that. She didn't know why either! We both whistled a little after.

qa.q: What did Dadi say girls shouldn't do?
qa.a: Whistle.

qa.q: Why did Damini feel angry and small?
qa.a: She was told to respect elders instead of getting a reason, which made her question feel wrong.

qa.q: How did Papa's explanation change things?
qa.a: He showed her respect is politeness, not fear, so she could ask Dadi gently. 😊

qa.q: What is Dadi's reaction to the polite question like?
qa.a: She laughs, admits she never knew why, and even whistles with Damini.

grounding: It illustrates a child told to respect elders without reasons and learning respect is courtesy, not silence.

passage: At harvest time in their village in Madhya Pradesh, Disha, eleven, listened to her father and grandfather argue about when to plant. She said the radio had forecast early rain. Her grandfather frowned. "Children should respect elders." Disha went quiet, her cheeks hot. Later, her uncle Rafiq sat with her by the well. "Respect means speaking kindly and listening. It doesn't mean you have no voice." The next morning, Disha brought her grandfather his tea and said gently, "Dada, the radio said rain on Tuesday." He paused, sipped, and nodded slowly.

qa.q: What did Disha bring her grandfather the next morning?
qa.a: His tea.

qa.q: Why did Disha's cheeks go hot?
qa.a: She felt shut down and embarrassed when told to respect elders without being told why.

qa.q: What made her second try go better?
qa.a: She spoke gently and kindly, as her uncle suggested, so her grandfather could listen.

qa.q: What might the grandfather's slow nod mean?
qa.a: That he heard her and may consider the forecast, even if he doesn't say so.

grounding: It shows a child told to respect elders without reasons, then learning respect is courtesy, not silence.

passage: In the school staff room, fifteen-year-old Gopika waited by the door, holding her notebook. In history class, Mr. Siddharth had given the wrong year for a treaty. She had wanted to correct him in front of everyone, but her friend whispered, "Don't, he's senior." Why couldn't a student correct a teacher who was wrong? She'd decided to try it differently. When he came in, she said quietly, "Sir, I think the treaty was 1802, not 1812. Can I show you my notes?" He checked, frowned, then smiled. "You're right. I'll correct it tomorrow. Thank you for telling me here and not in class."

qa.q: Which year did Gopika think was correct?
What question was bothering Gopika?
qa.a: Why a younger person cannot correct an elder who is wrong.

qa.q: Why did Gopika's approach work?
qa.a: She raised the correction privately and politely, with evidence, so the teacher could hear it.

qa.q: How does Mr. Siddharth feel about her choice of place?
qa.a: Grateful; he thanks her for telling him in the staff room rather than in class. 🙂

grounding: It shows a teen questioning why a younger person cannot correct an elder, and doing it privately and respectfully.

passage:
Dear Binita Mami,
I've been thinking about Diwali dinner. When you said girls shouldn't study engineering, I wanted to argue right there, but everyone told me to keep quiet and respect my elders. I still don't understand why I'm expected to stay quiet when something an elder says isn't fair. So I'm writing instead, because I do respect you. My friend topped her engineering entrance this year, and I'm applying next year too. I'd love for you to meet her when she visits. I hope you'll think about it. I'd rather disagree kindly than stay silent and feel resentful.
Your niece, Shreya

qa.q: What did Binita Mami say at Diwali dinner?
qa.a: That girls shouldn't study engineering.

qa.q: Why did Shreya write rather than argue at dinner?
qa.a: She disagreed strongly but thought a private, respectful letter would be heard better than a public argument.

qa.q: What makes this letter respectful without being silent?
qa.a: She states her view clearly, gives a real example and invites a meeting, while saying she respects her aunt. 🙏

qa.q: How might Binita Mami feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Maybe surprised, but more open to thinking about it than after a public argument.

grounding: It illustrates a teen questioning a rule of respect and choosing respectful private disagreement.

passage: I'm Raghav. In my strict joint family, at sixteen, I kept asking, "Why can't I tell my grandfather he's wrong?" He used to say unfair things about people from other communities. Once, at a family lunch, I shouted at him in front of everyone. My aunt Jyoti went pale, the room froze, and he didn't listen to a word. A month later, I sat with him alone on the terrace and said, "Dada, can I tell you about my friend Imran?" I told him how Imran's family helped us when Papa was in hospital. He listened. He didn't change overnight. But he listened.

qa.q: What was the name of Raghav's friend?
qa.a: Imran.

qa.q: Why did Raghav keep asking why he couldn't correct his grandfather?
qa.a: He felt his grandfather's comments about other communities were unfair and wanted to be allowed to challenge them.

qa.q: Which approach worked better, and why?
qa.a: Talking alone and calmly with a true story, because it let his grandfather listen without losing face in front of the family.

qa.q: How did the family lunch feel for Aunt Jyoti?
qa.a: Tense and alarming; she went pale when Raghav shouted.

grounding: It shows a teen questioning rules of respect and learning that private, respectful disagreement is heard better.

passage:
Respected Sabina Khala,
Thank you for your advice about my career at Eid. I know you want my future to be safe, and I truly value your experience. I see it differently, though. You feel a government job is the only secure path. I want to try a two-year design course first. I've saved enough for one year's fees from tuition work, and I have a backup plan if it doesn't work out: I'll sit the exams the year after. I hope you can hear this as my honest view, not as disrespect. May I visit you on Sunday and show you my portfolio?
With respect and love,
Vinita

qa.q: How did Vinita save for the course fees?
qa.a: From tuition work.

qa.q: How does Vinita want her aunt to hear the letter?
qa.a: As an honest view, not disrespect; she keeps a warm, respectful tone while disagreeing.

qa.q: What makes Vinita's disagreement easy for an elder to accept?
qa.a: She thanks her aunt, uses I see it differently, and shows a clear plan and backup. 🙂

qa.q: What might Sabina Khala feel when she reads it?
qa.a: Perhaps worried still, but respected and more willing to listen.

grounding: It shows a young adult disagreeing with an elder using respectful words and a calm, planned tone.

passage: People ask me how I talk to my grandfather about politics without a war. I'm Bhavna. For years I either stayed silent at dinner or we shouted. Neither worked. At twenty, I tried something new. I still call him Dadaji. I keep my voice low. I listen to his whole point first. Then I say, "Dadaji, I see it differently," and explain my view in two or three sentences, no more. My cousin Ujjwal thought I'd given up arguing. I hadn't. I'd just stopped fighting. Last week Dadaji said, "Tell me again why you think so." That felt huge.

qa.q: What did Dadaji say last week?
qa.a: Tell me again why you think so.

qa.q: Why did Dadaji's question feel huge to Bhavna?
qa.a: It showed that her calm, respectful way of disagreeing was finally being heard. 😊

qa.q: What steps does Bhavna follow when she disagrees?
qa.a: Keep the title Dadaji, speak softly, listen fully first, then say I see it differently and explain briefly.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal misread Bhavna's change?
qa.a: He thought she had given up arguing, when she had only stopped fighting.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult keeping honorifics and calm tone while disagreeing with an elder.

passage: I watched my cousin Payal, twenty-one, handle Naveen chacha at the wedding in Jaipur. He announced, loudly, that she should be married within a year. Everyone waited for her to go silent or snap back. Instead she said, "Chachaji, I respect your concern. I see it differently. I want to finish my master's first." Her voice was calm. He grumbled but nodded. Later at the buffet he even asked what her master's was about, and she told him about her research on water supply in small towns. I don't know what she felt inside. But she didn't look scared. She looked sure.

qa.q: What is Payal's research about?
qa.a: Water supply in small towns.

qa.q: How did Payal seem when she answered her uncle?
qa.a: Calm and sure, not scared, though the cousin cannot know what she felt inside.

qa.q: What choice did Payal make that others expected her not to?
qa.a: Instead of going silent or snapping, she kept the respectful title and calmly stated her own plan.

qa.q: How did the talk change Naveen chacha's behaviour later?
qa.a: He asked about her master's at the buffet, showing he had heard her. 🙂

grounding: It shows a young adult disagreeing respectfully with an elder, neither obeying nor rebelling.

passage: Mentor's note, analytics team. Dolma, twenty-four, our newest analyst, calls every senior sir or madam and never interrupts. In Monday's review I saw her frown at a wrong figure on Mr. Lalit's slide, open her mouth, then close it. Afterwards she asked me, "Was keeping quiet respect, or was I just scared?" I said the two can go together: respect is in the tone, not in the silence. We practised one line: "Sir, may I check one number?" On Thursday she used it, voice shaking a little. Mr. Lalit checked, called finance and corrected the slide on the spot, then thanked her in front of everyone.

qa.q: What did Mr. Lalit do after Dolma's question on Thursday?
qa.a: He checked, called finance, corrected the slide on the spot and thanked her in front of everyone.

qa.q: What was Dolma unsure about after Monday's review?
qa.a: Whether her silence was respect or fear.

qa.q: What does the mentor mean by respect is in the tone?
qa.a: You can speak up with a polite, careful tone and still show full respect.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team see Dolma's Thursday question?
qa.a: As careful and brave, and a sign it is safe to speak up politely.

grounding: It shows a young employee wondering whether silence is respect or fear and learning to speak up politely.

passage: Journal, 10 June. In today's meeting, Varun sir asked if anyone had concerns about the vendor plan. I had three. I said nothing. I call everyone sir and madam and nod along, like Appa taught me: never question seniors. Tonight I keep wondering: was that respect or fear? Because the plan will cause problems for the client, and I'll be the one fixing them in July. Tomorrow I'll email him politely: "Sir, may I share two concerns about the vendor plan?" I'll keep the third for when I have the numbers. My heart is racing just writing this. — Raghav

qa.q: How many concerns did Raghav have about the vendor plan?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: Why is Raghav's heart racing?
qa.a: Speaking up to a senior goes against what Appa taught him, and he fears it may seem disrespectful.

qa.q: What makes his email plan a good first step?
qa.a: It is polite and specific, and he saves the third concern until he has numbers. 🙂

qa.q: How might Varun sir see the email?
qa.a: Probably positively, since he asked for concerns in the meeting.

grounding: It illustrates a young employee questioning whether silence is respect or fear and planning to speak up politely.

passage:
Eshaan: meeting was so frustrating today
Mahima: why, what happened
Eshaan: Mehta sir said the deadline is next Monday. it's impossible. I said nothing
Mahima: you always say nothing 😅
Eshaan: I know. I don't want to seem rude. he's so senior
Mahima: is it respect or is it fear tho?
Eshaan: …honestly both
Mahima: you can be polite and still speak. "Sir, can we discuss the timeline? I want to make sure we deliver properly."
Eshaan: ok that sounds respectful actually
Mahima: try it tomorrow. I'll back you up with the testing numbers
Eshaan: okay. nervous but okay 🙏

qa.q: When did Mehta sir say the deadline is?
qa.a: Next Monday.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan stay silent in the meeting?
qa.a: He did not want to seem rude to a senior, and he admits it was both respect and fear.

qa.q: What line did Mahima suggest, and why does it work?

passage: I'm Vandana's neighbour, and I was at their flat when her relatives turned up without warning. Vandana, sixteen, had her board exam in two days and was bent over her chemistry book. Her mother called, "Vandana, chai banao!" She closed the book and went. Her brother Tarun, seventeen, stayed on his phone in the next room, and nobody called him. Then her little cousin needed a plate, her aunt wanted water, her uncle asked for more sugar. I saw her glance back at the book twice. Later, on the stairs, she said, "I don't mind serving guests. I mind that it's always me."

qa.q: What subject was Vandana studying?
qa.a: Chemistry.

qa.q: What did Vandana mean by it's always me?
qa.a: She values honouring guests but feels it is unfair that she serves while her brother is never asked.

qa.q: What could the family try so hosting is fair?
qa.a: Share the serving between Vandana and Tarun, especially during exams.

grounding: It shows a teen pulled from study to serve guests while a brother is left alone, raising fairness.

passage: Before: In March, whenever guests came, fifteen-year-old Swati was called to make tea, even during exams. Her brother Jomon kept playing football outside. During: In April, with her board exam the next morning, relatives arrived at seven. Swati was called again. She went, but in the kitchen her eyes filled with tears. Her grandmother saw and followed her in. After: That night her grandmother told her mother firmly, "Guests matter. So does fairness. Jomon can serve next time." In May, Jomon made the tea, spilled some, laughed, and Swati kept studying.

qa.q: What was Swati's brother doing when guests came in March?
qa.a: Playing football outside.

qa.q: Why did Swati's eyes fill with tears in April?
qa.a: She had an exam the next morning and felt it was unfair that she always had to serve. 😔

qa.q: What did the grandmother do that changed things?
qa.a: She valued hospitality but spoke up clearly for fairness between Swati and Jomon.

qa.q: What is serving tea like for Jomon in May?
qa.a: New and a bit clumsy; he spilled some and laughed.

grounding: It illustrates a teen daughter always serving guests while her brother is free, and a family moving toward fairness.

passage: Let me tell you something, Gopika, about when I was your age. Whenever relatives came, I was pulled from my books to make tea and fry pakoras. Your uncle Chinmay, my brother, sat with the men and talked cricket. I loved our guests. I loved feeding them. But I hated that it was always me. Once I missed revising for a big maths test because of it, and I got my lowest mark that year. I never forgot that. So last week, when guests came and your brother carried the tray without being asked, I was so happy I almost cried. Hosting is good. Sharing it is better.

qa.q: What did the elder fry for guests?
qa.a: Pakoras.

qa.q: How did the elder feel about always serving guests?
qa.a: She loved the guests but hated that the serving always fell to her and not her brother.

qa.q: Why did the brother carrying the tray move the elder so much?
qa.a: It showed hosting being shared fairly in a way she never had. 😊

qa.q: How might Chinmay remember those evenings?
qa.a: Probably as pleasant cricket talk, without noticing his sister's missed study time.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling always serving guests while a brother did not, and valuing fairness today.
